You are the geotechnical engineer. Two buildings are going up on an imaginary site in Budapest: a three-storey residential building and an eight-storey office building with two basement levels. Each of the nine lectures of the course is a station, and at each one you have to solve a real design question. With every approved station the model grows too, from getting to know the ground to the last floor slab.

Why do you need to understand the ground?

A developer has bought this site in Budapest and wants to put up two buildings on it. On the left, near the slope, there will be a three-storey residential building (Building A); on the right, an eight-storey office building with two basement levels (Building B). The positions of the buildings have already been set out.

You are the geotechnical designer. We know nothing about the ground yet: the section is still grey. Before we find anything out, take a guess! We will compare your guesses with the results at the end of the semester.
How much will the foundation under one of the columns of Building A settle?
And Building B? What kind of foundation do you expect?
What mainly decides whether a shallow or a deep foundation is needed?
The depth of the bearing stratum and the allowable settlement

The load of the structure matters, but on its own it does not decide: the same building can stand on a shallow foundation on dense gravel, but only on piles on thick soft clay. That is why you have to get to know the ground first.
Setting out done. Guesses: ${st.tips.tipS ?? '–'} mm settlement under a column of Building A; foundation of Building B: ${esc(st.tips.tipB ?? '–').toLowerCase()}.

Three boreholes (F1, F2, F3) and a cone penetration test (CPT) have been made, each reaching below the bearing stratum. The groundwater table is at −3.0 m. You can view the borehole logs on the section and here too.
At what depth does the bearing sandy gravel start?
It starts at the same level in all three boreholes. Depth is measured from ground level.
The top of the sandy gravel is at −9.0 m.
Which borehole went through organic soil (peat)?
F3 went through peat between 2.8 and 5.8 m. This is right below the footprint of Building B – one of the most important findings of the semester.
The CPT cone resistance is q<sub>c</sub> ≈ 0.9 MPa between 1.2 and 7.1 m, and q<sub>c</sub> ≈ 11 MPa between 7.1 and 9.0 m. What are these two layers?
Both are sand, only their water content differs

The low cone resistance points to a soft cohesive soil, the ten times greater value to a denser granular layer. The CPT stands near the boundary between the sand and the clay, so here the sand starts deeper than at F1.

Soil profile: fill 0–1.2 m; sand on the left and soft clay on the right down to 9.0 m; a peat lens below Building B between 2.8 and 5.8 m; sandy gravel 9.0–18.0 m; hard clay below. Groundwater −3.0 m.
What foundation is needed, and how deep?

Building A has a reinforced concrete frame with columns 8 m apart. The central column carries a permanent load of G<sub>k</sub> = 750 kN and a variable load of Q<sub>k</sub> = 220 kN. We design a square pad footing in the sand, with a 0.6 m thick reinforced concrete base.
What determines the depth of the foundation level?
The bottom of the fill (1.2 m): the foundation must sit in the bearing sand
The top of the sandy gravel (9.0 m)
We do not found on fill. Below the 1.2 m thick fill the footing is embedded further into the sand, so the foundation level is −1.8 m. This is below the frost line and above the groundwater.
What is the effective vertical stress (q′) at foundation level, beside the footing?
q′ = Σ γ·h from ground level down to foundation level. The groundwater is deeper than the foundation level.
What is the design bearing resistance (R<sub>d</sub>) of the B = L = 2.0 m footing?

R<sub>k</sub>/A′ = 0.5 · B′ · γ′ · N<sub>γ</sub> · s<sub>γ</sub> + q′ · N<sub>q</sub> · s<sub>q</sub>. For φ′ = 32°, N<sub>q</sub> = 23.18 and N<sub>γ</sub> = 27.72; for a square footing s<sub>q</sub> = 1 + sin φ′ and s<sub>γ</sub> = 0.7. The groundwater is 1.2 m below the foundation level, which falls between 0.5 · B′ and 1.5 · B′, so γ′ has to be interpolated linearly between 10 and 18 kN/m³. Finally R<sub>d</sub> = R<sub>k</sub> / 1.4.
Use the calculator to find the smallest footing width, rounded to 10 cm, for which the bearing resistance is still sufficient.
Drag the slider and watch the utilisation: Λ ≤ 1 is required.
The bearing resistance is more than enough even for the 2.0 m footing: its size is decided by settlement (station 5).

Foundation level −1.8 m (below the fill, in the sand). Central pad footing 2.0 × 2.0 m: R<sub>d</sub> = ${fmt(B2.Rd, 0)} kN, V<sub>d</sub> = ${fmt(B2.Vd, 0)} kN, Λ = ${fmt(B2.L, 2)}. For bearing resistance alone, ${fmt(BMIN, 1)} m would already be enough.

Wind applies a horizontal force to the pad footing, and the deep basement of Building B will reach into the groundwater. On the left edge of the site there is a 5 m high slope with a gradient of 1 : 1.5.
Sliding: what is the design sliding resistance (R<sub>d</sub>) at the base of the 2.0 m footing if the wind load is H<sub>k</sub> = 40 kN?

In drained conditions R<sub>d</sub> = V′<sub>k</sub> · tan δ<sub>k</sub> / γ<sub>R;h</sub>. V′<sub>k</sub> is only the permanent load (896.4 kN); for cast-in-place concrete δ<sub>k</sub> = φ′<sub>k</sub> = 32°, γ<sub>R;h</sub> = 1.1.
Uplift: the underside of the base slab of Building B will be at −7.6 m. What is the water pressure there?
u = γ<sub>w</sub> · h<sub>w</sub>, where h<sub>w</sub> is the water column above the underside of the slab. The groundwater is at −3.0 m.

During construction the basement structure (base slab and two floor slabs) has a self-weight of 40 kPa. How many kPa of permanent load are missing for safety against uplift, as a characteristic value?
UPL: γ<sub>G;stb</sub> · G<sub>k</sub> ≥ γ<sub>G;dst</sub> · U, where γ<sub>G;stb</sub> = 0.9 and γ<sub>G;dst</sub> = 1.0.
Until at least two more storeys have been built on top, dewatering must not be switched off – or the piles must also be designed for tension.
Which design approach do we use to verify the overall stability of the slope and Building A?
No verification needed, because the building is 10 m from the slope

According to the Hungarian National Annex, overall stability is verified with DA-3: the shear strength parameters are divided by partial factors. For a building near the crest of a slope this cannot be omitted.

Sliding: H<sub>d</sub> = 60 kN ≤ R<sub>d</sub> = ${fmt(RD_SL, 0)} kN. Uplift of Building B: u = 46 kPa below the slab at −7.6 m; during construction 11.1 kPa of permanent load is missing, so dewatering continues until the second storey is complete. Overall stability: DA‑3.
How much, and how unevenly, will it settle?

Now we find out how much the 2.0 × 2.0 m central pad footing settles. Settlement is calculated with the characteristic load (G<sub>k</sub> + Q<sub>k</sub>). The stress distribution below the centre of the footing is taken with Steinbrenner’s method; the influence depth is where the additional stress drops to 20 % of the effective geostatic stress.
What is the net contact pressure (σ<sub>0</sub>)?
σ<sub>base</sub> = (G<sub>k</sub> + Q<sub>k</sub>) / A, then σ<sub>0</sub> = σ<sub>base</sub> − q′.
Read the influence depth (m<sub>0</sub>) off the graph, measured downwards from the foundation level!
Where the orange curve (additional stress) crosses the blue curve (20 % of the geostatic stress).
m<sub>0</sub> ≈ ${fmt(MID.m0, 1)} m below the foundation level, i.e. about ${fmt(1.8 + MID.m0, 1)} m below ground level – still in the sand.
Layer summation: what is the settlement of the pad footing?
s = Σ Δh · Δσ<sub>mean</sub> / E<sub>oed</sub>. The table gives the stresses row by row; each row is 0.5 m thick (the last one less).
The edge column (G<sub>k</sub> = 450 kN, Q<sub>k</sub> = 130 kN, also on a 2.0 m footing) settles ${fmt(EDGE.s, 1)} mm; the two columns are 8 m apart. What is the angular distortion: β = 1/…?
β = Δs / L, where Δs is the difference between the two settlements and L is the distance between the columns. Enter the denominator.
This is smaller than the 1/500 limit: it does the frame no harm.

σ<sub>0</sub> = ${fmt(MID.q0, 1)} kPa; m<sub>0</sub> ≈ ${fmt(MID.m0, 1)} m; settlement of the central column ${fmt(MID.s, 1)} mm, of the edge column ${fmt(EDGE.s, 1)} mm; β = 1/${fmt(BETA, 0)} – OK. Your guess was ${st.tips.tipS ?? '–'} mm.
What if the ground is your biggest opponent?

Below the footprint of Building B there is a peat lens between 2.8 and 5.8 m, surrounded by soft clay. What if Building B were also put on a shallow foundation, a raft at 1.5 m depth? Below the wide raft the additional stress is about 90 kPa even at the level of the lens.
peat: thickness at the centre of the lens
How much would the peat lens alone be compressed?
s = Δσ · h / E<sub>oed</sub>. Mind the units: 0.8 MPa = 800 kPa.
This is seven times the allowable 50 mm – and the peat then goes on creeping for years.
The lens lies below only part of the building. What is the greatest danger?
Large differential settlement: the building tilts and cracks
The peat dries out and hardens
Nothing, because the raft evens out the difference
The stiffness of the raft cannot bridge such a large differential settlement. The building tilts towards the lens and the structure cracks.
What is the right solution for Building B?
Soil replacement in place of the peat
Preloading, then a shallow foundation six months later
Piled foundation down to the sandy gravel starting at −9 m

Soil replacement would mean excavating to 5.8 m, 2.8 m below the groundwater, and the peat keeps creeping even after preloading. The piles carry the load through the peat and the soft clay into the bearing gravel.

Under a shallow foundation the peat lens would be compressed by about 35 cm, unevenly. Decision: Building B goes on piles reaching down to the sandy gravel. Your guess: ${esc(st.tips.tipB ?? '–').toLowerCase()}.
What else acts on the foundation?

The excavation and the piles of Building B will be 15–20 m from Building A, which will already be standing. An unheated bicycle shelter will also be built next to Building B, on a light strip footing on soft clay.
How deep must the foundation level of the bicycle shelter be?
0.3 m, because the building is light
At least 0.8 m, below the frost line

Clay is frost-susceptible: a foundation above the frost line is lifted by frost and dropped back in spring. In Budapest, foundations in cohesive soil must be at least 0.8 m deep – being light does not protect the building; in fact it heaves more.
Which pair of techniques spares the neighbouring Building A most from vibration?
Driven steel sheet piles and driven precast piles
Vibrated sheet piles and Franki piles
Soldier pile wall and driven steel piles

The diaphragm wall is excavated with a grab and the CFA pile is drilled, both without vibration. The vibration from driving and vibrating can densify the sand and cause settlement below the neighbour’s foundations.
Bicycle shelter: foundation level at least 0.8 m, below the frost line. Building B is built with vibration-free techniques (diaphragm wall, CFA piles), so that Building A is not damaged.
When is a shallow foundation not enough?

Building B will stand on CFA piles 80 cm in diameter. The piles run from the basement base slab (−7.6 m) down to −17.0 m: 1.4 m in soft clay and 8.0 m in sandy gravel. For the calculation we use the illustrative unit values of the simulator in the Deep foundations module – you will learn the real design of piles in a later course.
At z = 17 m, q<sub>b</sub> = 5000 + 50 · 17 = 5850 kPa; R<sub>b</sub> = q<sub>b</sub> · π · D² / 4.
What is the shaft resistance in the sandy gravel (R<sub>s</sub>)?
q<sub>s</sub> is 69 kPa at 9 m and 77 kPa at 17 m, with a mean of 73 kPa; R<sub>s</sub> = q<sub>s,mean</sub> · π · D · L.
The section in the clay adds another 15 · π · 0.8 · 1.4 = ${fmt(PILE.Rc, 0)} kN.
Which part provides the greater share of the pile resistance?
R<sub>b</sub> ≈ ${fmt(PILE.Rb, 0)} kN, R<sub>s</sub> ≈ ${fmt(PILE.Rs + PILE.Rc, 0)} kN: roughly two thirds of the load is transferred to the gravel by the base.

CFA piles: D = 80 cm, between −7.6 and −17.0 m. Illustrative resistance: R<sub>b</sub> ≈ ${fmt(PILE.Rb, 0)} kN, R<sub>s</sub> ≈ ${fmt(PILE.Rs + PILE.Rc, 0)} kN; the load is transferred to the gravel mainly by the base.
How do we get down safely?
The two basement levels of Building B need a 7.6 m deep excavation, 4.6 m below the groundwater table, in soft clay, close to the site boundary and to Building A.
Which excavation support do you choose?

There is no room for a slope, and the groundwater would not allow one either. A soldier pile wall is not watertight, and a cantilever sheet pile wall is not enough for an excavation deeper than 4–6 m. The diaphragm wall is watertight and stiff, is built without vibration and can form part of the permanent basement wall.
Put the construction steps in order! Tap them in the right sequence.
Building the guide walls and the diaphragm wall
Excavation to below the first anchor row
Drilling and stressing the first anchor row
Excavation to final level, with dewatering
Casting the base slab on the pile heads
First the wall is completed, then excavation and anchoring follow each other level by level. Digging may only continue below an anchor row once the row above is stressed and holding.
Where should the fixed (grouted) length of the ground anchors go?
Directly behind the wall, in the soft clay
Beyond the potential slip surface, in the sandy gravel
Into the peat lens, because it is easy to drill
Into the fill, near the surface

The fixed length has to lie outside the sliding soil wedge, in a bearing stratum: here, the sandy gravel. That is why the anchors are long and inclined, and why permission is needed for them to extend below the neighbouring plot.

Anchored diaphragm wall, two anchor rows, fixed lengths in the sandy gravel. Sequence: diaphragm wall → excavation and anchoring level by level → dewatering → base slab on the pile heads. Then Building B goes up.

Across nine stations you have got from the grey, unknown ground to two finished buildings. Building A stands on pad footings in the sand at a depth of 1.8 m, with a settlement of about ${fmt(MID.s, 0)} mm per column. Because of the peat lens, Building B stands on CFA piles, and its two basement levels were built in an excavation supported by an anchored diaphragm wall.
The finished site can be seen once all nine stations have been approved. Until then you can walk around what has been built so far.
